subject: Rejoice! RESULTS OF THE QUESTIONNAIRE are here!!! YAY!

messages.author: d2a04571097d2bcb
messages.subject: Rejoice! RESULTS OF THE QUESTIONNAIRE are here!!! YAY!
parts:
Hello everyone,

I'd like to thank everyone for filling the questionnaire. Now, the future is not a murky dark unknown anymore, but a clear path for us to follow... :o)

First, we never discussed the official language of the mailing list, and this is something we should do. I'm currently writing in English as this forum has international membership, which will hopefully increase with other international students in the future. However, I understand that some people will not feel comfortable or confident enough to use English. My suggestion is to use both Slovenian and English interchangably, and get Google Translate to smooth the differences. The translations are sometimes horrible, but should get the message across. People with other suggestions are welcome to voice them.

So, I'll present a summary of the questionnaire. I'll try to keep it short, without any comments - sort of like the "results" section of a paper. I'll keep the discussion and (most of) personal comments  for  the e-mail discussion that should follow.  The entire questionnaire is still available here for you to look at and enjoy, but I locked it for editing.

All in all, 31 people answered the questionnaire out of the ~50 signed into the mailing list.

It seems that there are 10 people (32%) that use R (3-5 on the scale), four people (13%)  that use R every now and then (2 on the scale) and 17 (55%) that don't use R... yet.

The self-perceived knowledge (confidence in use of R) is similar… 7 people (23%) feel they know how to use R (3-5 on the scale), 14 people (45%) know the first steps (2  on the scale) and 10 people (32%) don't have a clue. Actually, some of the people in the "first steps" group are probably being too modest, so the actual base of experienced or semi-experienced users might be somewhat higher.

7 people are willing to teach beginners classes, but they are not necessary the ones that indicated they know how to use R.

19 (61%) people would like to have meetings once per month, 9  (29%) said that they'd like to meet every two weeks, one said every week, and one didn't reply to this question. Also, there was one interesting suggestion classified as "other" to have beginners meetings every two weeks as long as they are neccessary, and advanced meetings every month besides. An interesting point was made that more frequent meetings, every two weeks, would result in a more relaxed discussion as we'd get to know one another better.

All but one agree to have separate beginners/advanced user meetings. Regarding participation, 16  (52%) people would go only to beginners meetings, one person only to advanced, and 13 (42%) people to both meetings. One person didn't provide an answer.

An interesting question is the expectations - what people expect of the Rcoholic meetings. There is a large group that wants to learn R (22 people - 71%). 21 people (68%) would like to get some help with data analysis through the meetings, or have an interesting discussion about data analysis. 19  people (61%) would like an interesting discussion about R. A small, but vocal group of seven (23%) demands free coffee. There is a single voice crying out for free cocoa. A refreshment of exising R skills, helping hints from other users and info on new tools/packages were also mentioned.

Now, there is a long and diverse list of problems/techniques that people use or would like to use R for: statistical modelling - LM / GLM / GLMM and other regressions, genetics, mark-recapture, spatial analysis and simulations, making graphs, correlations, ANOVA, multivariate analyses, hypothesis testing, data processing in ethological and ecological research, testing community patterns, time series analysis, information-theoretic approach to model selection, model averaging, GOF tests for models, analysis of Q-PCR data, microarray analysis, habitat selection, spatial distribution of species with regard to habitat and interspecific interactions, modelling changes in communities caused by various environmental factors, conservation-ecological problems, classical tests, population modelling, exploratory data analysis, direct and indirect gradient analysis, minimum spanning trees, UPGMA. So, we got diversity down quite well. :) Not many people provided what sort of organisms or other topics they work on, so I'm skipping that.

There is a long list of suggestions and comments regarding the organization of meetings. I hope I'll get most of them: 

1) Interactive, hands-on meetings with people working on actual data . That came up a lot.  Homework also came up several times . Go figure. :o)

2) Separated begginers/advanced meetings (there seems to be a wide agreement on that point in the questionnaire).

3) Possiblity of people to present their own problems or work through their own data.

4) More frequent meetings for beginners until they stop being beginners.

5) Posting examples and code from the presentations/exercises online after meetings.

6) Known main topics of meetings before the meetings.

7) There was also an idea about starting an internet forum, as this is more permanent than the mailing list.

8) Idea for people to bring their R books to the meetings to show them to others.

9) A "how-to" part on each meeting where people would ask how to do something, and other people would answer (presumably there is always someone that knows the answer… :o)).

10 To rotate "teachers" - an individual or a pair would prepare a topic and teach it to everyone that wishes to learn.

11) There was a long list of praise for the effort of starting the Rcoholics. Most of these should go to Maarten, who actually came up with the idea in the first place and saw it through.

So, here it is. Now, a discussion!

Tomaž
